column1: # THE STRING BUILTINS (G9 phase 6, docs/design/TEMPLATE.0.md D4, D5).
#   esc(s, variant?)      make `s` safe inside a literal
#   usc(s, variant?)      read it back out
#   rep(s, pattern, sub)  replace every match
#   split(s, sep)         a list of fields
# Every expectation below was obtained by running BOTH engines and
# diffing. That matters more here than almost anywhere else in the
# suite: the host functions these could have been built from disagree
# about every part of the job -- `JSON.stringify` escapes what Go's
# encoding/json does not, `encodeURIComponent` is not RFC 3986,
# JavaScript's split INSERTS a pattern's capture groups where Go's does
# not, and the two read a substitution template differently. So both
# ports spell every convention and both matching loops out by hand, and
# these rows are what holds them to the same answer.
# THE DEFAULT CONVENTION IS THE C ESCAPE, JSON CANONICAL, which covers
# TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin,
# Scala and JSON itself -- one convention rather than a lookup. A
# control character with no short form becomes `\uXXXX`; a character
# that was already safe is untouched, which is what makes escaping by
# A VARIANT NAMES A CONVENTION, NOT A LANGUAGE, and that is why it is a
# variant rather than something a renderer knows: several languages
# share one convention and one language has several -- a C-family
# literal escapes differently in each quote, and SQL spells a literal
# one way and an identifier another. `esc(s, regex)` is the one whose
# output is itself checked by another part of the language: it always
# answers a pattern the portable subset accepts.
# AN UNKNOWN VARIANT IS A REFUSAL AT THE CALL, never a pass-through: a
# new convention arrives by NAME rather than by a silent change in what
# `usc` IS THE LEFT INVERSE, AND IT IS PARTIAL. `usc(esc(s))` is `s`
# for every `s` and every convention -- the rows below are that law, one
# per variant. The other direction does not hold: several spellings
# escape to one value, so `esc(usc(t))` is `t` only for canonically
# TEXT WITH NO ORIGINAL IS REFUSED rather than answered with a
# different string. A lone surrogate is refused in both ports because it
# is not a character either can carry; a lone quote is refused where the
# convention doubles it, because its meaning depends on what was meant
# to follow; and a bare `&` is refused because it opens an entity, where
# a bare regex metacharacter passes because it does not.
# `rep` REPLACES EVERY MATCH. A replace-the-first default is a footgun
# in a generator that normalises separators, and anchoring is how a
# document asks for one. The pattern is the portable subset `re()`
# takes, so one document has one regexp language; the substitution is
# A SUBSTITUTION NAMING NOTHING IS A REFUSAL, not an expansion to the
# empty string: a generator that writes a file with a hole in it and
# says nothing is the failure this refusal exists to close. `$0` names
# A PLAIN STRING SEPARATOR IS A LITERAL and an `re(...)` is a pattern.
# The asymmetry with `rep` is deliberate -- splitting is usually on a
# literal -- and it removes the trap where `split(v, ".")` silently cuts
# between every character. Empty fields are PRESERVED, so `join` is the
# inverse; an empty separator yields the code points, not the UTF-16
# units a host split would give.
# THE CHAIN THE DESIGN NAMES: a generator derives names as much as it
# interpolates them, and these are the steps that get from a pin to the
# words a derived name is built out of.
# UNFIRED, a string call canons as its CALL, which reparses to the same
# value -- so canon convergence holds for a model that has not
# finished. Reaching that state takes an argument that never settles
# (`1+true` is the stuck operation budget.tsv uses).
